takeaways: Operating earnings fell 5.8% to $12.705 billion, about $5.94 per Class B share on 2.14 billion average equivalent shares — a few cents above the $5.91 Zacks consensus, which had already baked in the decline.

Insurance was the drag: underwriting profit tumbled 43% to $1.35 billion as GEICO's losses rose 8.5% and underwriting expenses jumped 17% (Bloomberg), and insurance investment income fell 14% to $2.73 billion on lower short-term rates.
Everything else grew: BNSF earned $1.73 billion (+19%), Berkshire Hathaway Energy $1.61 billion (+8%), and manufacturing, service and retailing $4.04 billion (+12%).
Greg Abel bought back about $9.6 billion of Berkshire stock in Q3, more than double Q2's $4.5 billion, for about $14.4 billion so far in 2026.

The cash pile still grew to $377.4 billion; excluding rail and utility cash and T-bill payables it was $352.3 billion, down 1.9% from Q2 (CNBC). Net earnings, including stock-portfolio gains, fell 28% to $22.1 billion — a number Berkshire itself calls 'usually meaningless.'
verdict: Profits slipped, the Street saw it coming, and Abel answered by buying back stock at more than twice the pace of last quarter — a loud 'we think we're cheap' from a company that's up 13% this year while tech melts. GEICO had a rough quarter and lower rates nicked the float income, but trains, power and factories all grew. Max's take: boring in the best way, and the buyback is the headline. The stock gets its first vote Monday.
